newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PRESS DIGEST-Hong Kong Newspaper Headlines-Jan 27.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Hong Kong Newspaper Headlines-Jan 27.

text.p: These are some of the leading stories in the Hong Kong press on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

-- APPLE DAILY -- The name of the former director of Immigration Laurence Leung has been put down on the "security lookout list" by Canadian customs, which means that if Leung enters Canada, customs officials have to report to their superiors and seek instructions.

-- A factory owned by three Hong Kong businessmen has been attacked four times by local villagers and facilities worth $1m have been destroyed. The villagers accuse the owners of being money-minded and of ignoring the fact that factory waste has been damaging the environment of the village.
-- WEN WEI PO --Beijing officials warned against new actions by Taiwan's pro-independence groups.

-- A retired official in China's Henan province is cycling around 50 cities to promote awareness of Hong Kong's handover. He had covered 2,700 km. Along the way he gives lectures by the roadside and to diners in restaurants.
-- ECONOMIC JOURNAL -- The government's measures to dampen property speculation has seen some effect, but the sale of new developments is still going well.
-- MING PAO -- Chinese officials say the Communist Party Central Committee has no intention to make Shenzhen a free port. Shenzhen would continue to be a special economic zone.
-- SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST -- Members of the provisional legislature would be banned from United States soil under a controversial proposal by a Senate committee.
-- Embarrassed by complaints from trading partners, Beijing has threatened to remove export rights from any company found dumping goods in international markets.
-- HONGONG STANDARD -- Hong Kong's current building boom has provided a favourable environment for the construction business to launch initial public offerings.

-- The Hong Kong Tourist Association says uncertainty over security in post-handover Hong Kong could result in a lot of empty hotel rooms in the territory unless effective steps are taken to offset the growing concerns.
